summary:
TerraPath is a GPS for crop rotation. A farmer taps a plot on a map and the app proposes three rotation routes for the next three seasons. Each route is scored 0–100 on water, soil and safe harvest, with the reasons behind each score in plain English. Many smallholders repeat the same crops out of habit, while frost, late rains and El Niño years shift the planting window. NASA Earth data is free, but it rarely reaches the farmer as a decision.

TerraPath answers “Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data” by changing the rotation, not just the season. It turns 44 years of daily NASA POWER climate and NASA SRTM elevation, plus FAO crop references, into transparent, rule-based options the farmer can compare offline on a phone. When an input is missing, it says “unknown” instead of guessing. In a 2016–2024 backtest, the routes needed 6–32% less water than growing maize every year at all four sites that produced routes.
details:
How it works.

  1. Locate the plot. Altitude and slope come from NASA SRTM at 30 m. If the terrain is too rugged for the climate grid, the app shows a mountain warning.
  2. Read the climate. NASA POWER gives daily rain, temperature and radiation from 1981 to 2024. From these the engine computes frost days per month, rainfall variability, dry years and FAO-56 reference evapotranspiration (ET₀).
  3. Build every rotation. A 16-crop library is filtered by FAO EcoCrop temperature, rain and altitude limits. The engine then lists every three-season sequence that passes, including one with a fallow season: 204 sequences in Huancabamba, Piura.
  4. Score each sequence from 0 to 100.
  • Water: crop demand (FAO-56 Kc × ET₀) against rain.
  • Soil: legumes, botanical-family changes between seasons, and cover crops.
  • Safe harvest: frost below each crop’s lethal temperature, rainfall variability and dry years.
  1. Pick three routes. The engine keeps the Pareto front and shows the best route for the farmer’s priority (water, soil or safe harvest). Each route is compared with what the farmer grows today and carries its reasons.

Validation. Routes were chosen with 1981–2015 data only, then replayed on 2016–2024. The baseline was maize grown every year, the crop with the most harvested area in each country according to FAOSTAT. Total water deficit over 2016–2024:

  • Huancabamba (Peru): 942 vs 1,138 mm.
  • Piura sur (Peru): 1,691 vs 1,808 mm.
  • Iowa (US): 1,494 vs 1,870 mm.
  • Nakuru (Kenya): 1,208 vs 1,773 mm.

The routes did not change when the weight on water moved from 20% to 80%. 193 automated tests pass.

The app. An installable web app that works offline. It has a map of the sites with data and three onboarding questions: where, what grows now, what matters most. It then shows three routes with score bars, a “Why this route?” screen (frost by month, rain vs. crop needs), a sowing calendar with a downloadable reminder, and a “My farm” view by week, month and year in a normal year. It is in English. The language selector is built, and the translation is waiting for a native speaker.

Tools. The engine is written in Python. It uses pandas and PyArrow for tables, requests and earthaccess for NASA downloads, rasterio, h5py and pyhdf to read SRTM and HDF files, and Plotly for report figures. A Jupyter notebook walks through the whole engine, and pytest plus Node.js run the tests. The app is HTML, CSS and JavaScript with a service worker, a Leaflet map and OpenStreetMap tiles, and no Google APIs. Every downloaded file keeps a provenance record with its URL, size and SHA-256 hash. The app screens are documented in Figma.

Goals. Give smallholder farmers options with reasons instead of orders. Keep every number traceable to a dataset. Say “unknown” when an input is missing instead of guessing.

Current state and limits (stated openly).

  • The engine runs on six sites: three in Piura (Peru), Iowa (US), Nakuru (Kenya) and California’s Central Valley (US).
  • The same top route (alfalfa › barley › potato) wins at four very different sites. The crop library is still too small to tell those climates apart, and it does not yet include quinoa or local varieties.
  • In Piura, GPM IMERG gives about twice NASA POWER’s annual rain (834 vs 467 mm in Huancabamba). The scores use POWER until station data shows which source is right.
  • Two sites produce no routes. In Piura norte, SRTM puts the plot at 2,864 m but the climate grid at 878 m, so no rotation passes. In California, water demand is unknown for the crops that pass the filter.
  • Of the 16 crops, 8 lack a verified FAO-56 Kc and 6 lack a lethal frost temperature, so those scores show “unknown”.
  • SMAP and MODIS files were empty after download. None of the Sentinel-2 NDVI values pass quality checks. FAO GAEZ layers have an unverified legend. None of these enter the scores.
  • There are no plot-level yield, soil or irrigation records. Routes are screening options, not agronomic recommendations, and have not been reviewed by an agronomist.

Next steps.

  1. Settle the POWER vs IMERG rain difference in Piura with SENAMHI station data.
  2. Add Andean crops (quinoa, local potatoes) with verified Kc and frost limits.
  3. Get an agronomist to review the rules and local planting calendars.
  4. Add languages by native speakers, a listen button, and more districts.
